phenolphthalein_1pct.note: Simplified schematic - matches molecules/phenolphthalein.svg's caveat. Not a bond-precise organic structure; see the properties card note.

zn_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/zn.svg's caption.

mg_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/mg.svg's caption.

fe_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/fe.svg's caption.

cu_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/cu.svg's caption.

ca_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/ca.svg's caption.

mgo_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many magnesium and oxide ions, not a molecule.

hno3_1m.note: The nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

na2co3_1m.note: The carbonate group is flat - carbon and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

caco3_s.note: One calcium ion with one carbonate ion. The real solid is a lattice of many of these, not a molecule.

cuo_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many copper and oxide ions, not a molecule.

nh4cl_1m.note: The ammonium ion is tetrahedral - the four hydrogens point to the corners of a triangular pyramid.

co2_g.note: Carbon dioxide is linear - the two oxygens sit exactly opposite each other at 180 degrees.

nh3_g.note: Ammonia is pyramidal, not flat: the lone pair on the nitrogen pushes the three hydrogens down to about 107 degrees apart.

fecl3_0_1m.note: Drawn with the three chlorides spread evenly around the iron. In solution the ion is surrounded by water molecules as well.

baso4_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many barium and sulfate ions, not a molecule.

agi_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many silver and iodide ions, not a molecule.

agbr_s.note: One ion pair, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many silver and bromide ions, not a molecule.

feoh3_s.note: Three hydroxide ions spread evenly around the iron, which carries a 3+ charge here rather than the 2+ of iron(II) hydroxide.

pbcl2_s.note: One lead ion with two chlorides, drawn simply. The real solid is a lattice of many such ions, not a molecule.

rust_s.note: An Fe2O3 unit with one water molecule shown loosely attached. Rust genuinely has no fixed formula - the amount of water varies from place to place in the same flake, which is why it is written Fe2O3 with a dot and xH2O.

nacl_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many sodium and chloride ions - and because those ions are locked in place, the solid does not conduct.

na_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/na.svg's caption.

s_powder.note: A single atom, drawn simply. Solid sulfur is really made of rings of eight atoms, not single ones.

c_s.note: A single atom. In charcoal and coal, many carbon atoms are joined into sheets and networks rather than separate molecules.

n2_g.note: The two atoms are held by a triple bond - the strongest part of the reason nitrogen is so unreactive.

so2_g.note: Bent, not linear - the lone pair on the sulfur pushes the two oxygens down to about 119 degrees apart.

no2_g.note: Bent like sulfur dioxide, and the only common coloured gas in this lab.

h2co3_aq.note: The carbon and its three oxygens all lie in one flat plane.

hno3_aq.note: The nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

cahco3_aq.note: A calcium ion with two hydrogencarbonate ions. Only one oxygen of each group is drawn attached to the calcium, to keep the picture readable.

h2o2_aq.note: The molecule is not flat - the two hydrogens sit on either side of the O-O bond like a half-open book.

mno2_s.note: One manganese ion with two oxide ions. The real solid is a lattice of many of these, not a molecule.

v2o5_s.note: Drawn simply as two vanadium atoms sharing five oxygens. The real solid is a layered network, not a molecule.

pt_s.note: A single atom, not a molecule - the catalyst gauze is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/pt.svg's caption.

so3_g.note: Flat and perfectly even - sulfur in the middle with its three oxygens 120 degrees apart, all in one plane.

kclo3_s.note: The chlorate ion is a pyramid - the chlorine sits above the triangle of its three oxygens, not in the middle of it.

kcl_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many potassium and chloride ions.

nh4cl_s.note: The ammonium ion is tetrahedral - the four hydrogens point to the corners of a triangular pyramid.

na2co3_s.note: The carbonate group is flat. The real solid is a lattice of many sodium and carbonate ions.

nh4no3_s.note: An ammonium ion beside a nitrate ion. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

kno3_s.note: The nitrate group is flat. The real solid is a lattice of many potassium and nitrate ions.

cacl2_s.note: One calcium ion with two chlorides. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

naoh_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a lattice of many sodium and hydroxide ions.

cao_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a lattice of many calcium and oxide ions, not a molecule.

cuso4_anhydrous_s.note: The same copper and sulfate ions as the blue crystals, but with no water in the structure at all - which is exactly why this one is white.

cuso4_5h2o_s.note: Two of the five waters are drawn, arranged round the copper ion. In the real crystal four sit around the copper and the fifth is held by the sulfate - and it is that built-in water which makes these crystals blue.

cocl2_s.note: Cobalt with two chlorides and no water at all, which is what makes this form blue.

cocl2_6h2o_s.note: Two of the six waters are drawn. In the real crystal all six surround the cobalt ion in an octahedron, and it is that shell of water which turns the blue form pink.

ag_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/ag.svg's caption.

pb_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/pb.svg's caption.

al_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/al.svg's caption.

cuno3_aq.note: Each nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

znno3_aq.note: Each nitrate group is flat - nitrogen and its three oxygens all lie in one plane.

al2o3_s.note: Two aluminium ions with three oxide ions, drawn simply. The real solid is a rigid lattice of many of these - which is why it does not conduct until it is melted or dissolved in cryolite.

li_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. Lithium is the least dense solid element there is.

k_metal.note: A single atom, not a molecule - a solid metal is a lattice of many of these. See molecules/k.svg's caption.

li2o_s.note: Two lithium ions to one oxide ion. Lithium is the only alkali metal that burns in air to this simple oxide.

na2o2_s.note: The two oxygens are still bonded to EACH OTHER - that surviving oxygen-oxygen bond is what makes this a peroxide rather than an oxide, and is why sodium parts company with lithium here.

mgco3_s.note: The carbonate group is flat. The real solid is a lattice of many magnesium and carbonate ions.

baco3_s.note: The same carbonate group as magnesium carbonate, with a much larger cation beside it - which is exactly why this one needs far more heat to break apart.

nabr_s.note: One ion pair. The real solid is a cubic lattice of many sodium and bromide ions.

nai_s.note: One ion pair. The iodide ion is the largest of the common halides, which is why it holds its outer electrons most loosely and reduces most readily.

nahso4_aq.note: A sulfate group that has kept ONE of its two hydrogens - which is why this salt still gives an acidic solution.

h2s_g.note: Bent like water, but at a wider angle of about 92 degrees - and unlike water it has almost no hydrogen bonding, which is why it is a gas at room temperature while water is a liquid.

agnh3_aq.note: The silver ion sits in a straight line between its two ammonia molecules. Holding it this way is what keeps a silver halide dissolved that water alone could not touch.

chloramine_g.note: Ammonia with one hydrogen swapped for a chlorine - pyramidal, like the ammonia it came from.

kscn_aq.note: The thiocyanate ion is linear - sulfur, carbon and nitrogen in a straight line.

fescn_aq.note: The iron holds the thiocyanate through its sulfur end. In solution the iron also carries water molecules that are not drawn here.

cu_nh3_aq.note: Four ammonia molecules arranged in a square around the copper ion. Each nitrogen also carries three hydrogens, drawn here for two of them only to keep the shape readable.

k2cr2o7_aq.note: Two chromium atoms joined through a single bridging oxygen - that bridge is what makes this the DIchromate rather than two separate chromates.

na2cro4_aq.note: One chromium with four oxygens in a tetrahedron. The chromium is in exactly the same +6 state as in dichromate - only the arrangement differs.

croh3_s.note: Three hydroxide ions around the chromium. This hydroxide is amphoteric - it reacts with excess alkali as well as with acid.

kmno4_aq.note: Manganese with four oxygens in a tetrahedron, in its highest oxidation state of +7.

k2mno4_s.note: The same manganese-and-four-oxygens unit as permanganate, but carrying two potassium ions instead of one - because the manganese here is +6 rather than +7.

ch4_g.note: A genuine tetrahedron - the four hydrogens point to the corners of a triangular pyramid at 109.5 degrees to each other, not to the corners of a square. Rotate it and that becomes obvious in a way the flat drawing cannot show.

ch3cl_g.note: Still tetrahedral, with a chlorine in place of one hydrogen. The chlorine is much larger, which is easiest to see by rotating the model.

c2h6_g.note: Two tetrahedral carbons joined by a SINGLE bond. That single bond can rotate freely, so the two ends spin relative to each other - something the double bond in ethene cannot do.

c2h4_g.note: FLAT. Every atom lies in one plane, and rotating the model shows it edge-on as a straight line. The double bond is what locks it that way - it cannot twist, which is why alkenes can have cis and trans forms and alkanes cannot.

c2h2_g.note: Perfectly LINEAR - all four atoms on one straight line. The triple bond allows nothing else, and rotating the model shows it stays a line from every angle.

cac2_s.note: A calcium ion beside a carbide ion, whose two carbons are triple bonded to each other. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

c2h4br2_aq.note: The carbons are tetrahedral again, and the bond between them now rotates freely - the double bond of ethene has gone, used up in taking the two bromines on.

c2h2br4_aq.note: Four bromines, two on each carbon - a triple bond can take two lots of bromine where a double bond takes only one.

c2h5oh_aq.note: Two carbons with an OH group on the end. That oxygen-hydrogen bond is the whole reason ethanol is a liquid that mixes with water, while ethane - the same two carbons without it - is an insoluble gas.

glycol_aq.note: An OH group on EACH carbon. Two of them means twice the hydrogen bonding, which is why this is thick and high boiling where ethanol is thin and volatile.

ni_s.note: A single atom, not a molecule - the catalyst is finely divided metal, a lattice of many of these with an enormous surface area.

c6h6_l.note: PERFECTLY FLAT. Rotate it and the whole ring goes edge-on to a single straight line - every one of the twelve atoms lies in one plane. All six carbon-carbon bonds are the same length too, which is the strongest evidence that there are no separate double bonds here: the electrons are spread evenly right round the ring.

c6h12_l.note: The same six carbons, and NOT flat. This is the chair form: alternate carbons sit above and below the mean plane, because every carbon here is tetrahedral. Rotate it beside benzene and the difference between a delocalised flat ring and a saturated puckered one is unmistakable.

c6h5br_l.note: Still flat, and still a complete ring - the bromine has replaced a hydrogen rather than breaking anything open.

c6h5no2_l.note: The nitro group lies in the same plane as the ring, so the whole molecule is still flat.

c6h5so3h_aq.note: A flat water-hating ring at one end and a water-loving acid group at the other - the two halves that make a detergent work.

c2h5br_l.note: Two tetrahedral carbons with a bromine on the end. The bromine is much bigger than the hydrogens, and it is the polarity of that carbon-bromine bond that makes the carbon open to attack.

c2h5nh2_aq.note: Pyramidal at the nitrogen, exactly like ammonia - and for the same reason, the lone pair pushing the other three groups down.

naoh_ethanolic.note: Chemically the same sodium hydroxide as the aqueous bottle - it is the ethanol it is dissolved in, not the reagent itself, that changes what happens to a halogenoalkane.

phenol_s.note: The OH sits in the same plane as the ring, and the whole molecule is flat. That flatness is not decoration - it is what lets the oxygen's charge spread into the ring once the hydrogen leaves, which is why phenol is an acid and ethanol is not.

c6h5ona_aq.note: Phenol with its hydrogen gone. The charge left on the oxygen is shared into the flat ring beside it rather than sitting on one atom, which is the whole reason this ion is stable enough to form.

ch3cho_l.note: Look at the carbonyl carbon: it carries a HYDROGEN as well as the oxygen. That hydrogen is the whole difference between this and propanone, and it is what makes an aldehyde easy to oxidise. The C=O group and everything attached to it lie in one plane.

ch3coch3_l.note: Now compare with ethanal: the carbonyl carbon here has a CARBON on each side and no hydrogen at all. There is nothing to take off without breaking the chain, which is exactly why ketones fail both Tollens' and Fehling's.

ch3cooh_aq.note: The COOH group: one oxygen double bonded to the carbon, one carrying the hydrogen. It is that O-H hydrogen that comes off as an ion, not any of the three on the other carbon.

ch3coona_aq.note: With the hydrogen gone, the two oxygens become identical - the charge is shared evenly between them, and the two carbon-oxygen bonds are the same length. That sharing is why the ion is stable and the acid can form at all.

ester_l.note: The acid's O-H hydrogen has been replaced by an ethyl group from the alcohol. That single swap is the whole of esterification, and it is why the smell changes so completely.

tollens_aq.note: The silver sits in a straight line between its two ammonia molecules. This is the same diammine arrangement that keeps silver chloride dissolved - here it is holding the silver ready to be reduced back to metal.

fehlings_aq.note: Fehling's is a MIXTURE, not a molecule, so there is no true structure to draw. What is shown is a copper(II) ion with the two oxygens of a tartrate gripping it - the arrangement that stops the copper precipitating out of the alkali. Treat this as a sketch of the idea rather than as a real geometry.

cu2o_s.note: TWO coppers to one oxygen, because the copper here is +1 rather than its usual +2. The real solid is a lattice of many of these.

pcl5_s.note: Turn it and you will see the five chlorines are NOT all alike: three sit in a flat triangle round the middle and two stick straight out top and bottom. That shape is called a trigonal bipyramid, and phosphorus can only manage five bonds at all because it has empty d orbitals - nitrogen, directly above it, never forms NCl5.

ch3cocl_l.note: The carbonyl carbon and the three atoms round it lie in one flat plane, which leaves it open from above and below. Add the chlorine pulling electrons away along its bond and that carbon becomes the most exposed one in the whole family - which is exactly why this compound reacts with cold water on contact.

anhydride_l.note: Two ethanoic acid units sharing the single oxygen in the middle. Compare the two carbonyl carbons with the one in ethanoyl chloride: here they have only an oxygen pulling on them, not a chlorine, so they are less exposed and the whole molecule is correspondingly gentler.

ch3conh2_s.note: The nitrogen, the carbon and the oxygen all lie in one plane, and the nitrogen is FLAT rather than pyramidal like the one in ammonia. That flatness is the visible sign of its lone pair being pulled towards the carbonyl - which is why ethanamide is neutral instead of basic, and why the peptide links in a protein are rigid.

glycerol_l.note: Three carbons, each carrying an OH. Those three OH groups are the attachment points for the three fatty acid chains of a fat, and they are also why glycerol grips water so well that it ends up in hand cream.

fat_l.note: A real fat has three chains of seventeen carbons each - far too many to draw usefully - so the chains here are SHORTENED. What is honest in this model is the plan: one glycerol on the left with three ester links coming off it, all three pointing the same way. Turn it and you can see why fats pack together so tightly, and why straightening or kinking those chains is the whole difference between a solid fat and a liquid oil.

soap_aq.note: The chain here is SHORTENED - a real soap tail is seventeen carbons long. What matters is the shape: a charged head at one end and a long greasy tail at the other. Turn it side-on and you are looking at the reason soap works, because the head can stay in the water while the tail buries itself in the grease.

detergent_aq.note: Same shortened tail as the soap model, and the same two-ended shape - but the head is built round a SULFUR rather than a carbon. Put the two models side by side: that one swapped atom is the entire reason a detergent lathers in hard water and soap does not.

urea_s.note: Turn it and the whole molecule is FLAT - both nitrogens, the carbon and the oxygen lie in one plane. That is the same flatness seen in ethanamide, and for the same reason: each nitrogen's lone pair is pulled towards the carbonyl. Urea simply has two of them instead of one, which is where its unbeatable 46 % nitrogen comes from.

nh42so4_aq.note: Two ammonium ions and one sulfate. Both ions are neat tetrahedra - turn the model and each looks the same from four directions - but they behave quite differently in water: the sulfate sits there unchanged while the ammonium slowly gives a hydrogen ion back, which is what makes the solution acidic.

sio2_s.note: This is a FRAGMENT, and the fragment is the lesson. There is no silica molecule to show - every silicon here has four oxygens round it and every oxygen bridges two silicons, and the pattern simply carries on past the edges of the model in all directions. To melt sand you have to break that network apart, which is why it takes 1700 degrees, while carbon dioxide with its similar-looking formula is a gas at room temperature.

clinker_s.note: One silicate tetrahedron with three calcium ions round it. The real clinker is a lattice of these repeated endlessly - what is shown is the repeating unit, the same way a single NaCl pair stands for a whole salt crystal. The calcium is what makes wet cement so alkaline, and so good at burning skin.

cement_set_s.note: There is no molecule of set cement, so this is a SKETCH of what hardening does: silicate units, shown as grey blocks, that have grown out and locked into each other through the space the mixing water filled. The number of water molecules taken up varies from place to place in the same lump, which is why set cement has no single formula. Nothing here dried out - the water became part of the solid.

alum_aq.note: One aluminium ion between two sulfates. Notice how SMALL the aluminium sphere is for something carrying three positive charges - that combination of small size and high charge is the whole story. It pulls so hard on the water molecules around it that they let go of a hydrogen ion, which is why a solution of this salt turns litmus red, and it is the first step towards the hydroxide floc.

aloh3_s.note: Turn this one and look at the SPACE in it. Aluminium hydroxide units bridged loosely through hydroxide groups, with wide gaps everywhere - that openness is the entire reason it works. A dense precipitate would drop straight to the bottom and leave the water as dirty as before, while this mesh forms through the whole depth and carries the clay and bacteria down inside itself.

glucose_aq.note: The hydrogens are left off so the ring can be seen. Turn it and the ring is not flat - it buckles into the shape called a chair, and every OH group sticks out sideways rather than up or down. That is what makes this particular arrangement the most comfortable of all the sugars, and it is why glucose, out of all of them, is the one life runs on.

sucrose_aq.note: Two sugar rings joined through the single oxygen in the middle. Find that oxygen and follow it to the carbon on each side: those two carbons are exactly the ones that would otherwise open into reducing groups, and both are used up making this one bond. That is the whole reason sucrose gives nothing with Fehling's. The hydrogens are left off, and the fructose ring on the right is drawn as a six-membered ring for clarity when the real one has five.

invert_sugar_aq.note: The same two rings as sucrose, but no longer joined - this is a MIXTURE of two separate sugars, not one molecule, and the gap between them in this model is real rather than decorative. Compare it with the sucrose model: one bond is missing, and that is the entire difference between a negative Fehling's test and a positive one.

gluconate_aq.note: The ring has opened out into a straight chain and the end carbon now carries TWO oxygens instead of one. That is the only change Fehling's made - the aldehyde has become a carboxylate - and everything else along the chain is the glucose it came from, untouched. Hydrogens are left off.

starch_aq.note: A real starch molecule has HUNDREDS of glucose units and could not be drawn. Five are shown, each as one grey block, with the linking oxygens between them in red. What is honest here is the plan and the curve: the chain does not run straight but twists, and that twist is what eventually coils it into the helix the iodine test depends on.

starch_iodine_aq.note: Turn this one and look down the length of it: the grey sugar units spiral round, and the purple iodines sit in a straight line down the hollow middle. They touch nothing - there are no bonds drawn to them because there are none. The colour comes from iodine being TRAPPED inside the coil, which is exactly why warming the tube, which shakes the coil loose, makes the blue-black vanish.

albumin_aq.note: A real protein has thousands of atoms, so each amino acid is shown here as one grey block with the peptide nitrogens between them in blue. The point of the model is the FOLD: the chain does not lie straight, it doubles back on itself into a particular shape, and everything the protein does depends on that shape being kept.

albumin_coag_s.note: Put this beside the albumin model and count the bonds: there are exactly as many, and not one has been broken. All that has changed is where the blocks sit - the neat fold has been shaken out into a sprawl. That is denaturation, and it is why cooking an egg cannot be undone by cooling it and why a biuret test on the result still works.

biuret_aq.note: Biuret reagent is a MIXTURE - copper(II) sulfate stirred into plenty of sodium hydroxide - so there is no real structure to show. What is drawn is a copper(II) ion with hydroxide ions round it, which is the state the copper is actually in while it waits for a protein. Read it as a sketch of the bottle's contents, not as a formula.

protein_cu_aq.note: One copper ion held by FOUR peptide nitrogens at once, two from each of two stretches of chain. Count them, because the number matters: a single amino acid has no peptide link at all and gives no colour, and you need at least three joined together before there are enough nitrogens to grip the copper. That is why the biuret test detects a protein rather than an amino acid.

scum_s.note: One calcium holding TWO shortened soap chains, one above and one below. Sodium could only ever hold one; calcium's second charge lets it bridge two, and the bridged pair has no charged end left free to keep it in solution. That is scum, and it is why it will not wash off.

h3po4_aq.note: Phosphorus at the centre of a tetrahedron of four oxygens, three of which carry a hydrogen - which is what makes the acid tribasic.
